title: The economic and environmental performance of biomass as an “intermediate” resource for power production
abstract: Electricity powered by biomass is expanding. We examine four recent biopower plants and global benchmarks to assess their overall performance, confirming the characterization of biomass as an “intermediate” resource for power production. Electricity from biomass is more expensive than energy efficiency, natural gas, wind, or solar but substantially less expensive than new coal or nuclear plants. Compared to coal and natural gas per MWh produced, the NOx and SO2 emissions of biopower are also intermediate. We confirm that current investments in biopower can be attributed to an array of stakeholder value propositions extending beyond basic economic and environmental metrics.

## The economic and environmental performance of biomass as an “intermediate” resource for power production

Marilyn A. Brown[∗] , Alice Favero, Valerie M. Thomas, Aline Banboukian

_School of Public Policy, Georgia Institute of Technology Atlanta, GA, USA_

A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T _Keywords:_ Electricity powered by biomass is expanding. We examine four recent biopower plants and global benchmarks to Biomass power plants assess their overall performance, confirming the characterization of biomass as an “intermediate” resource for Levelized cost of electricity power production. Electricity from biomass is more expensive than energy efficiency, natural gas, wind, or solar Biogenic carbon and air pollution but substantially less expensive than new coal or nuclear plants. Compared to coal and natural gas per MWh produced, the NOx and SO2 emissions of biopower are also intermediate. We confirm that current investments in biopower can be attributed to an array of stakeholder value propositions extending beyond basic economic and environmental metrics.

## **1. Introduction**

Global electricity generated from biomass more than tripled between 2000 and 2016, and is forecast to grow at an increasing pace through the year 2040 when it could account for 3.6% of the world's electricity (IEA, 2017, p. 257). In 2010, biomass generated 164 TW h (TWh) of electricity and accounted for 1.1% of world electricity generation. In 2016 biomass generation rose to 566 TWh and accounted for about 2% of world electricity generation with the United States leading, followed by China, Germany, Brazil (IEA, 2017, p. 257; REN21, 2017). China and Brazil are becoming increasingly important producers, benefiting from support programs for biomass electricity generation, in particular from agricultural residues (Brown and Sovacool, 2014; IEA, 2017).

Electricity generation from biomass in the United States has grown significantly over the past decade, increasing from 54.3 TWh in 2005 to 62.6 TWh in 2016, also benefiting from policy incentives (USEIA, 2017a, b). Much of the growth in biopower is occurring in southern states such as Virginia, Florida, and Georgia and is baseload and dispatchable (Mayes, 2016). For instance of the 545 MW (MW) of current biomass capacity in the United States that has been converted from coal plants, 373 MW (68%) is located in the Southeast (SNL Energy Database, 2017).

Given the continued political and economic interest and growth in biopower, this paper evaluates the economic and environmental performance of four Virginia biomass plants owned by Virginia Electric and Power Company (referred to as “Dominion”). Three of these plants were converted from coal plants in 2012 and one was purchased and expanded in 2004. Unlike plants that co-fire coal with biomass, which

have received comprehensive reviews in recent years (Agbor et al., 2014; Roni et al., 2017; Verma et al., 2017), dedicated biomass plants such as these four owned by Dominion have not received the same thorough treatment recently.

This article helps fill this gap by assessing the economic and environmental performance of four recent investments in biomass plants and comparing our findings to benchmarks in the literature using the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) and estimated emissions of NOx, SO2, and CO2 per MWh. Confirming the characterization of biomass as an “intermediate” resource for power production in terms of both economic and environmental performance, we explore the question of why this resource continues to compete in Virginia and beyond, by examining other motivating factors.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we describe Dominion's biomass plants in Virginia and the regulatory and policy context of these utility's investments. Section 3 describes the data and methodology used to assess the economic and environmental performance of the four biomass plants, and the role of other motivating factors. Section 4 presents the results, comparing them to an array of benchmark sources and including a sensitivity analysis of the results to key parameters such as discount rates and power plant lifetimes. Section 5 presents a discussion of the paper's findings and its conclusions.

the expansion of biomass power in Virginia and the Southeast. In 2004, Dominion purchased the Pittsylvania biomass facility that was completed by a prior owner in 1994, and Dominion expanded the plant's capacity from 83 MW to 90 MW.

In 2013, Dominion converted three of its coal plants to 100% biomass fuel. Located in Altavista, Hopewell, and Southampton, these plants were originally built as coal-fired power stations between 1989 and 1992. Each of these plants is rated at 51 MW, which is a typical size for dedicated biomass plants (IRENA, 2012).

These three plants and the Pittsylvania plant are evaluated in this paper and their performance is compared to benchmark statistics for the United States and elsewhere. In 2016, the full capacity of each of these generating units was available for power production between 63 and 78 percent of the hours of the year, and the plants were dispatched to produce electricity during most of the hours that they were available (Table 1). Based on their heat rates, the efficiency of these units ranges from 22.3 to 22.5 percent.[1] This is relatively low compared with the typical efficiency of direct combustion in stoker boilers according to IRENA (2012, p. 38), which is estimated to be 36 percent. In 2016, the Pittsylvania plant's equivalent availability factor was 60 percent, but its net capacity factor in 2016 was only 20 percent. The plant's relatively high heat rate made it less competitive for dispatch compared to the three biomass plant conversions (Table 1).

All four of Dominion's Virginia biomass plants examined in this paper have spreader-stoker boilers and use woody biomass or waste as feedstock. Thus, they are categorized as “open loop” facilities because they use biomass feedstocks that were not originally intended for use as a fuel source. Fuel costs comprise anywhere from 57 percent to 80 percent of total levelized costs, depending on the plant. An estimated 3300 tons of waste wood or about 150 truckloads are unloaded each day at the three biomass conversion plants, totaling approximately 600,000 tons of biomass per year. The Pittsylvania plant consumes approximately twice that amount, totaling about 1.2 million tons annually.

Dominion also operates the Virginia City Hybrid Energy Center (VCHEC), a 585 MW plant that co-fires coal with wood waste. VCHEC is the only coal co-firing plant in the Southeast that is currently combusting significant quantities of biomass in the absence of cogeneration. It is expected to gradually increase its biomass fuel to 10% by 2021 (Dominion Energy, 2017, pp. 33). Other power producers in Virginia are also using biomass. In 2012, Miller-Coors Brewing opened a biomass-based electricity plant in Elkton, Virginia, to dispose of brewing wastes, and in 2013, the Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative (NOVEC) commissioned a 50 MW wood waste biomass plant in South Boston, Virginia (Mayes, 2016).

These biomass power plant investments were made in the context of supportive state and federal renewable electricity policies. At the federal level, utilities have been able to take advantage of Production Tax Credits (PTCs). First created under the Energy Policy Act (EPAct) of 1992, PTCs have been renewed and expanded numerous times, including extensions in 2014, 2016 and 2018. The four plants examined here have been eligible for a PTC of $12/MWh during their first ten years of service.

At the state level, biomass power plants have contributed to Virginia's voluntary Renewable Portfolio Standard (RPS). In 2010, the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) issued a Final Order granting Dominion's request to participate in Virginia's voluntary Renewable Energy Portfolio Standards program, finding that “the Company has demonstrated that it has a reasonable expectation of achieving 12% of its base year electric energy sales from renewable energy sources during calendar year 2022, and 15% of its base year electric energy sales from renewable energy sources during calendar

## **3. Data and methods**

## _3.1. Economic assessment_

We begin by estimating the LCOEs of the four biomass power plants in Virginia, using the methodology described below. We then examine where these estimates fall within the range of costs estimated in reviews of comparable biopower plants. Finally, we examine the variable O&M costs per MWh of the four plants relative to the supply curve of the PJM wholesale electric market, to assess whether they have proven more or less expensive than electricity available for purchase in the region.

We assess the cost of competing supply-side and demand-side electricity resources to answer the question “are biomass power plants competitive with other electricity resources that Dominion could purchase today and over the lifetime of these plants?” The economic assessment ends with a sensitivity analysis of key parameters.

The LCOE of each plant is calculated as the annualized capital, operating and maintaining costs and fuel costs per MWh of electricity produced over the discounted lifetime of electricity generation. While LCOE estimates must be viewed in light of their assumptions, they provide a convenient indicator of the relative costs of different technologies and thus a practical way for comparing their level of competitiveness (National Academies of Sciences, 2016). ## _3.2. Environmental assessment_

To calculate the environmental performance of the four biomass power plants, we use the emissions rates of NOx and SO2 from the EPA, Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID) from 1996 to 2016.

Due to the longer atmospheric duration and greater complexity of CO2 emissions, we conduct a lifecycle assessment of the emissions of this pollutant from the four biomass power plants. Specifically, we use the global warming potential approach, which weights the impact of the biogenic carbon based on its lifetime in the atmosphere compared to the emission of fossil carbon (Guest et al., 2013).

We assume that all the power plants use softwood produced in the US southeast, with an age at harvest of 11 years. Site preparation, fertilizers, and harvesting together result in emissions of 2400 kg CO2e/ ha (Dwivedi et al., 2011). Products from a single stand include midsized trees mainly used for lumber, pulpwood, and logging residues. We assume for this calculation that both the pulpwood and the logging residues are used to make wood chips for the power plant. Based on data in Dwivedi et al. (2011), this comes to 75% of the 200 green tons per hectare harvested; the rest is used for lumber. Allocating by mass between the timber and the biomass used for wood chips, 18 kg CO2e per dry ton can be attributed to the wood chips from the growing and harvesting of the trees.

Considering a 50 km travel distance from the point of harvest to the chip mill, plus the empty return of the log truck, we calculate 4.2 kg CO2e per dry ton for transportation. Transport to the point of use may be another 50 km; if the truck is the same as the logging truck this contributes an additional 4.2 kg CO2e per ton of dry wood chips.

We assume a diesel chipping machine that uses about 1.67 L of diesel fuel per ton of wood (Westbrook et al., 2006). Drying the biomass can consume 1800 Btu per pound of evaporated water (Worley, 2011), equivalent to 4.2 MJ/kg of water evaporated. This is assumed to be accomplished with wood heat. With a typical energy density for dry wood chips of 18 MJ per kg, an additional 0.23 kg of wood chips will be needed for each finished kg of wood chips.

## **4. Results**

## _4.1. Levelized cost of electricity from biomass power plants_

In this section, we present the results of the LCOE analysis for the four Virginia biomass power plants. We estimate LCOE with and without renewable energy certificates (RECs) to assess the impact of the certificate on the total costs. Under the base case (without RECs), the LCOEs of the four Dominion biomass plants range from $93 to $143/ MWh. In the scenario in which power plants receive RECs, the LCOEs are lower by 7–10% depending on the plant. With RECs, LCOEs range from $83 to $133/MWh, with a simple average of $96/MWh (Table 4).

Altavista has the highest LCOE largely because of its higher biomass feedstock costs (almost twice the other three plants). The Altavista plant also required a slightly higher upfront investment cost. In addition, it has a lower capacity factor and slightly higher annual fixed O& M costs than the other two converted biomass plants.

While the LCOE of the purchased biomass plant (Pittsylvania) is similar to two of the converted plants, the composition of its costs is quite distinct, with much higher fixed O&M costs and non-fuel variable

## _4.2. Comparison to reviews of typical costs for new biomass plants_

Table 5 provides a summary of the LCOE estimates for biomass direct generation in the literature. Some estimates refer to current values while others focus on future LCOE projections; some provide national

averages estimates while others provide global averages. The review suggests that LCOE estimates are influenced by several factors such as (i) different core biomass power generation technologies; (ii) capital, O &M and fuel costs estimates from different data sets and models; (iii) regional variations; (iv) alternative fuel costs scenarios; and (v) the assumed size of the power plant. Moreover, it shows that the LCOE for biomass direct generation is higher in Europe than in the United States.

The LCOE estimates of Dominion's four Virginia biomass plants ($93 to 143/MWh) fall within the range of international estimates published by IRENA (2012) for stand-alone spreader-stoker type biomass power plants ($60 to $210/MWh). The electricity from these power plants is indeed not more expensive than the average electricity costs presented in the literature. One of the four biomass plants (Altavista) falls above the $84.8 to 125.3/MWh range estimated by USEIA (2017a) for new plants in the United States entering service in 2022, where the range represents the minimum and maximum values across U.S. regions, subsidies are excluded, and the capacity factor is assumed to be 84 percent.

## _4.3. Comparison to PJM supply curve in 2016_

In competitive electricity markets, the bids offered for different types of electricity resources are indicative of their cost-competitiveness. The PJM Interconnection operates one of the largest wholesale competitive markets in the United States, covering all or parts of 13 states including Virginia and the District of Columbia. Representing approximately one-fifth of the U.S. wholesale electricity market, where a plant falls on the PJM supply curve of bids is a reliable indicator of its relative cost-competitiveness.

Because bids into the PJM market are confidential, we have developed a surrogate PJM supply curve for the year 2016 based on the variable O&M cost of power plants located in the PJM service territory. This supply curve serves as a rough proxy of the market competitiveness of Dominion's four Virginia biomass plants relative to other plants in the region (Fig. 1). By combining fuel costs and non-fuel variable O& M costs, and by classifying and color-coding the observations into eight types of primary fuels, it is possible to visually examine the cost-competitiveness of different types of plants.

As shown in Fig. 1, the four Virginia biomass power plants are situated on the inside elbow of the PJM supply curve. There are approximately 170 GW of electricity with variable O&M costs that are lower, including solar, wind, and hydro plants that have essentially no fuel costs. Approximately 20 GW of electricity generation available to PJM costs more on a $/MWh basis than the four Virginia biomass power plants. This PJM wholesale market analysis shows that the four Virginia biomass plants have relatively high O&M costs compared to other electricity resources available for purchase in the region. For perspective, the summer peak demand served by the PJM Regional Transmission Operator exceeded 160 GW in only in three of the 17 years from 2000 to 2016 (Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission, 2017) Thus, if these four plants were forced to compete in the PJM market, they might not operate except during unusually hot summers.

Solar, wind, and hydro plants occupy the least expensive left side of this supply curve because they have essentially no fuel costs and relatively low variable O&M costs. After natural gas and nuclear enter the supply curve, biomass, coal, and petroleum are the sources that represent the next highest variable O&M costs in the PJM region.

This type of comparison is most useful when evaluating the competitiveness of existing generation relative to power that could be purchased in competitive markets. When considering options for the construction of new capacity, the scope of consideration needs to go beyond variable O&M costs to include all of the categories of costs and considerations included in Table 3.

## _4.4. Comparison to alternative supply-side electricity resources_

In this section, we compare the costs of Dominion's biomass conversions to published LCOE estimates of non-biomass resources, including onshore wind, utility-scale solar, natural gas combined cycle, coal with carbon capture and sequestration, and nuclear. We rely on two organizations that provide LCOE estimates for alternative electricity resources in the United States: USEIA (2017a and 2018) and Lazard (2016, 2017); we supplement those estimates with the inclusion of a $10/MWh system integration costs associated with variable and non-dispatchable technologies (Brown et al., 2018). In addition, we examine Hammerschlag (2017), which compiles EIA's regional estimates for NEMS Region 16 (“Virginia-Carolina”) that enable more appropriate comparisons for Dominion's Virginia biomass plants. These estimates account for federal subsidies to non-biomass technologies, where applicable (Fig. 2).[2]

Our results show that Dominion's biomass conversions are not competitive with several other established sources of electricity. Fig. 2 shows the estimated total cost of producing electricity from natural gas, wind and solar ranging from $57 to $67/MWh in the Virginia/Carolina region. These values represent upper limits of LCOE estimates for these non-biomass sources. On the other hand, Dominion's lowest biomass conversion costs (namely those that exclude Altavista) are $84 to $85/ MWh, when accounting for the financial benefits of RECs and federal subsidies. ## _4.5. Comparison to energy-efficiency resources_

To compare the cost of biomass or other electricity supply options with the cost of reducing load levels, we review estimates of the cost of energy-efficiency resources. Four types of costs are generally considered: 1) the cost of any financial incentives needed to motivate consumers to use energy more efficiently, which is often benchmarked to the “energy-efficiency premium,” the cost of the added increment of energy efficiency; 2) the cost of providing information and technical assistance, which in some cases may be the bulk of the program costs; 3) program administration costs; and 4) financing costs that apply to energy-efficiency programs, as well as to electricity generation projects. A complete assessment of energy efficiency must also consider the role of the rebound effect as well as the market transformation context of programs and policies. In addition, energy-efficiency and demand-side management programs can have different load shape impacts, which influence their value to utility resource managers. The concept of an energy-efficiency “virtual power plants” is emerging, where the load shape consequences of different demand-reduction strategies are considered (Brown and Wang, 2015, pp. 130–132).

The State of Virginia has not commissioned a comprehensive assessment of the state's energy-efficiency potential. However, the costcompetitiveness of energy efficiency was well documented in the National Academy of Sciences (2010) assessment and in earlier studies by multiple national laboratories (Koomey et al., 1998; Brown et al., 2001). More recently, Hoffman et al. (2018) conducted a

comprehensive evaluation of energy-efficiency program impacts and costs in the United States. The study examined data from annual reports filed by program administrators of electricity efficiency programs funded by customers of investor-owned utilities in 41 states between 2009 and 2015. With costs of saved electricity (CSE) ranging from $15/ MWh in the Midwest to $33/MWh in the Northeast, electricity efficiency is found to be cost-competitive across all regions of the U.S. The 11 states in the U.S. South where CSE estimates were available, varied from a low of $16/MWh in Georgia to $48/MWh in Florida. A simple average CSE across these 11 states is $26/MWh ($2016). This is the estimate for energy efficiency we display in Fig. 2.

In addition to considering the cost-effectiveness of energy-efficiency improvements, utility planners need to know that sufficient resources are available. Baatz and Barrett (2017) evaluated the LCOE saved by the EmPower Maryland energy-efficiency programs from 2008 through 2015. They concluded that the programs produced 51 million MWh of energy savings at a levelized cost of $34/MWh. These savings are more than twice the 20-year lifetime of electricity generation from the four Virginia biomass plants. Similarly, low LCOEs for energy efficiency have been documented by a range of programs implemented across the United States, addressing the energy waste in homes, businesses, and industry, and documenting 200 TWh of electricity efficiency potential available at less than $30/MWh (Brown and Wang, 2015, Figure 7.4).

In sum, the results of a large body of research evaluating the costeffectiveness of demand-side programs (starting in the 1990s) suggest that the investing in energy efficiency would likely have been less expensive than the cost of generating electricity from Dominion's four biomass plants in Virginia or indeed from alternative supply-side options for capacity expansion.

The median value of these 25 LCOEs for each of the four plants is shown by red a diamond in Fig. 3. ## _4.7. Emissions of NOx, SO2, and CO2_

In this section, we present estimates of the environmental impacts of the power plants in terms of rates of two primary local air pollutants – oxides of nitrogen (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO2) per electricity produced. This section also presents a lifecycle calculation of the effect of converting coal plants to biomass plants in terms of CO2 emissions.

Power generation from fossil fuels, biomass and waste contribute to emissions of air pollutants that adversely impact public health and the environment. The amount of pollution that a power plant emits depends greatly on its combustion design, level of the emissions controls, and the nature of the feedstock used in the facility.

Fig. 4 shows the emissions rates of NOx and SO2, per MWh of electricity generated from biomass, coal, and natural gas, based on four authoritative sources. Generally, biomass feedstocks have intermediate levels of NOx and SO2 relative to fossil fuels, producing less than coal, but more than natural gas on a per MWh basis. The figure also shows the 2016 emissions rates of the four biomass power plants analyzed in this paper, based on data from EPA's Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID). Their estimates are well below the average in the case of SO2 and exactly in line with the median of the studies surveyed for NOx.

Fig. 5 shows the chronology of SO2 and NOX emissions rates of the four Virginia biomass plants from 1996 to 2016. The conversion of Altavista, Hopewell, and Southampton from coal-fired power stations to 100% biomass fuel in 2013 produced a significant reduction in the amount of NOx/MWh. Comparing their emissions of NOx per MWh in 2012 with their rate in 2014, Hopewell and Southampton show a reduction of 50–62%. There are no data available for Altavista in 2012, but comparing them with the 2010 rate, the level was reduced by 37% in 2014 and by 99% in 2016. The temporal trend in the rate of SO2 is different because of the addition of scrubbers (environmental control technologies) to the coal plants prior to their conversion to biomass.

Because Pittsylvania began operation as a biomass plant in 1994, its NOX and SO2 rates were relatively constant from 1998 to 2016 and in the range of the rates presented in the literature.

Biomass power generation also emits carbon dioxide (CO2) and other greenhouse gases. When biomass grows, carbon dioxide is absorbed from the atmosphere, and this same carbon is released as carbon dioxide when the biomass is combusted. In addition, the processing of the biomass to make it into fuel, its transport to the power plant, and changes in soil and land use all contribute to the net lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions of biomass fuel.

While the carbon dioxide released from the combustion of the biomass is the same as the carbon absorbed by the biomass when it was growing, the time lag between growing and combusting and regrowing new stands of trees means that biomass combustion results in higher levels of CO2 in the atmosphere for a period of time. One way this has been accounted for is through the global warming potential approach, which weights the impact of the biogenic carbon based on its lifetime in the atmosphere compared to the emission of fossil carbon (Guest et al., 2013). The global warming potential for 11-year biomass with no storage and with a 100-year time horizon is 0.04. The fraction of dry wood biomass that is carbon is approximately half (Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), 2005).

The CO2 emission from combustion of the biomass is 1.83 kg CO2 per kg dry biomass. Therefore, the CO2e emissions are 0.04 times that, or 0.08 kg CO2 per kg biomass.

In some biomass energy systems, land use change resulting from increased demand for biomass can result in additional CO2e from disruption and transition of soils and ecosystems. In other biomass energy systems, cultivation of biomass can add to the stock of carbon in soils and land. For the case of southern timberland, there is currently no evidence of forestry increasing the net carbon stock in soils, and there is no evidence of ecosystem disruption outside of timberland for local wood chip production. There has been concern that rich, primal forests might be harvested, contrary to the assurances of forestry companies; that scenario could indeed result in higher emissions and impacts, and is not included in these calculations. In total, we estimate the emission of 138 kg of CO2e per ton of biomass or 7.7 g CO2e per MJ of wood chips.

To compare this to the emissions from coal-fired power plants, both the direct emissions as well as the upstream emissions associated with mining, transporting and preparing the coal must be considered. The direct emissions, based on the heat rate of the power plants and the reported CO2 emissions from eGrid, are 45 g CO2 per MJ of coal input. The upstream emissions contribute, on average, an additional 50% (Whitaker et al., 2012) for a total of about 68 g CO2e/MJ of coal. This is more than eight times the lifecycle emissions of the biomass fuel. Expressing these on a per-kWh basis, the coal plants emitted approximately 1000 g CO2e/kWh, and the biomass-powered plants emitted about 110 g CO2e/kWh.

## _4.8. The role of other value propositions_

In this section, we document Dominion's planning assumptions and value propositions based on testimony filed on behalf of Dominion and the Virginia SCC. Most of the information in this section is drawn from Dominion's case concerning its three coal plant conversions.[3] The available information is limited in three important respects.

First, it does not include a comparative analysis with a broad range of alternatives to biomass conversion.[4] The analysis of planned costs documented in Dominion's case before the Commission focuses on the cost-effectiveness of converting the three Virginia coal plants to biomass compared to continuing to operate them as coal units. In its planning process, Dominion compared the cost of the biomass

However, these cost estimates are redacted and are unavailable to the public (Dominion, 2011, p. 14/58). Dominion concluded that future revenue requirements would be less than they would otherwise be if the conversions did not occur (Tufaro, 2011).

The testimonial evidence and Dominion's application in 2011 provide estimates of $388 million to $434 million “net present value savings” to customers when compared to the continued operation of the coal plants. As stated by a witness for Dominion Virginia Power, “The Biomass Conversions are expected to provide $388 million (NPV) in value to our customers” (Dominion, 2011, pp. 35, 54). A senior analyst in the Virginia SCC's Division of Energy Regulation, noted that Dominion's application states that “estimated net present value savings include the value of PTCs, the sale of RECs, and carbon legislation” delivering a customer savings of approximately $434 million (Dominion, 2011, pp. 16, 58). These estimated savings do not necessarily infer a reduction in Dominion's future revenue requirements; they simply estimate that the company's future revenue requirements would be less than they would otherwise be if the plants continued to operate on coal (Tufaro, 2011). By narrowly delimiting their assessment to either conversion to biomass or continued coal plant operations, Dominion failed to reveal that more cost-effective options were available.

The available testimony and public documents make clear that Dominion saw coal-to-biomass plant conversions as delivering a significant improvement in functionality by switching three coal plants from peaking to baseload performance. A witness for Dominion Virginia Power stated that “The Company will transform existing generation facilities that are not being fully utilized, modify them, and enhance their utilization and value to customer” (Dominion, 2011, pp. 35, 54). As coal units, the peaking plants supplied electricity only 18 percent of the time, mostly when demand increased significantly on hot and cold days. As biomass plants, Dominion hoped that their availability factors could increase to 92 percent (Ruppert, 2013). However, based on recent operating data, this goal has been only partially achieved. Specifically, the net capacity factors of the three converted biomass plants ranged from 63 percent to 68 percent in 2016 (Table 3), higher than the coal peaking units, but significantly lower than the 92 percent forecast. The shortfall may be due to the biomass plants' lack of cost competitiveness relative to the PJM market.

It is clear that other motivating factors played a role. In addition to references to expanding baseload capacity, testimonies and associated documents refer to the value of increasing fuel diversity (Ruppert, 2013; Dominion, 2017). Job creation and local economic development also were noted by Dominion to be motivating factors, along with providing environmental benefits consistent with Virginia's voluntary Renewable Portfolio Standard ( Dominion, 2017, p. 36).

The expected value of PTCs and RECs was also noted by Dominion in its application and testimonies as enabling the economic operation of the converted plants. Glenn A. Kelly, Director of Generation System Planning for Dominion, stated that “When repowered to operate on biomass fuel, the lower combined fuel and emissions costs, along with the expected federal Production Tax Credits (or “PTCs”) and renewable energy certificates (“RECs”), are expected to enable the converted power stations to run economically at baseload capacity factors” (Dominion, 2011). However, based on our analysis, it appears that even with these public subsidies and environmental credits, Dominion's biomass conversions are not competitive with several other established sources of electricity, all of which are more environmentally attractive than coal.

This paper illustrates the problem of stranded assets, which are investments that must be retired before the end of their economic life due to changing regulations or technologies. Because of their shorter-thananticipated operational lifetimes, they can become unable to deliver an economic return (IEA, 2013). As coal plants, the three Virginia plants

examined here could have become stranded. Since the purchase of these plants was approved by the Virginia SCC, if the assets were stranded, their cost would likely have been recovered through rates charged to customers. Their conversion to biomass extended their operational lifetimes, but significant upfront capital investments were required. This case study exemplifies the potentially significant role of stranded investments as economies transition in response to changing regulations and environmental imperatives (IRENA, 2017).

## **5. Discussion and conclusions**

We find that four biomass plants in Virginia, and U.S. biomass plants overall hold an intermediate position in terms of both economic and environmental performance. Compared to the coal plants from which three of the four plants were converted or new coal plants that could be built today, emissions of NOx, SO2, and CO2 are all substantially lower on a per MWh basis. However, they are higher than emissions from nuclear, solar, or wind power, which all have nearly zero emissions on a lifecycle basis. The comparison with natural gas plants is more nuanced – biomass plants produce more NOx and SO2 but less CO2 per MWh (Bruckner et al., 2014, Figure 7.6).

In terms of cost, the biomass power plants are intermediate because they are less costly than new coal or nuclear power plants, but more expensive than new natural gas, wind, or solar plants. Biomass power plants are dispatchable and can provide baseload power that is better able to follow loads and thereby provide more reliability and flexibility to the power system than coal, nuclear, solar, and wind.

Specifically, we estimated the levelized cost of electricity generated from Dominion's four biomass plants in Virginia: three that were converted from coal plants in 2012 and one that was purchased by Dominion in 2004. In the base case, which includes the value of PTCs, the LCOEs of the four plants average $106/MWh, and with RECs included they average $96/MWh. Altavista has the highest LCOE, largely due to its greater biomass feedstock costs and higher annual fixed O&M costs. As a result, unlike the other three plants, the LCOE estimate for Altavista falls outside the range of costs estimated by USEIA and Lazard for comparable new stand-alone biomass plants. The results of a sensitivity analysis focused on alternative assumptions reinforce our findings.

Our analysis of the PJM wholesale market substantiates that Dominion's four Virginia biomass plants are more expensive than electricity available for purchase from alternative sources in the region. Comparing variable O&M costs for the PJM capacity market in 2016, we find that the four Virginia biomass power plants are situated on the inside elbow of the PJM supply curve. Although approximately 170 GW of electricity costs less, the summer PJM peak rarely exceeds 160 GW. Solar, wind, and hydropower plants occupy the least expensive left side of this supply curve because they have essentially no fuel costs. After natural gas and nuclear enter the supply curve, biomass, coal, and petroleum represent the next highest variable O&M costs in the PJM region.

We also assessed whether Dominion's four biomass plants are providing competitive electricity resources compared with alternative resources that Dominion could purchase over the lifetime of these plants. In this comparison, we include an upper limit estimate of $10/MWh of integration costs for solar and wind based on values from the literature. Adding these estimates to published LCOE estimates for utility-scale electricity technologies suggests that biomass is more expensive than natural gas combined cycle, solar, and wind resources. Estimates of the LCOE for energy efficiency indicate that demand-side investment is the least expensive option.

A review of publicly available information led us to conclude that Dominion's planning process did not fully evaluate a broad range of alternatives to coal plant conversions to biomass. The plant conversions were seen as delivering a significant improvement in functionality by switching the plants from underutilized coal peakers to more flexible

baseload performance. They were also viewed as helpful to meeting Virginia's voluntary Renewable Portfolio Standard and to generating local economic benefits, such as jobs from the use of a labor-intensive, locally resourced fuel. Nevertheless, the broader scope of costs and benefits from a wider array of alternatives received limited emphasis in public testimonies and supporting documents.

When Dominion first considered converting Virginia coal plants, U.S. markets were just beginning to see significant domestic supplies of low-cost natural gas, the cost of wind power was declining but not yet competitive, and solar photovoltaic systems were experiencing significant cost and performance breakthroughs. The potential benefits of large-scale investment in cost-competitive energy efficiency were well documented in national studies in 2010 and earlier, although few states in the Southeast had scaled-up their demand-side programs and documented their ability to offset or delay the construction of new power plants. It is likely that investing in natural gas plants would have resulted in lower revenue requirements and reduced costs to consumers in Virginia, but natural gas plants would not have contributed to Virginia's voluntary renewable energy goal.

Our results suggest that in today's energy marketplace, additional plant conversions from coal to biomass in Virginia would not be the least-cost renewable option. The economics were not competitive in 2012, and they would be even more unattractive in today's marketplace with cheap natural gas, declining wind and solar costs, and an abundance of affordable energy efficiency.

The results presented in this study of four Virginia biomass power plants should not be generalized to all power production from biomass. Local biomass fuel costs are highly variable and result in site-specific economic opportunities for biopower. And technologies and fuels are rapidly evolving. Nevertheless, our evaluation methodology is replicable, and our results are consistent with benchmark U.S. and

international estimates. Thus, our approach could greatly assist the much needed ongoing economic assessments of future biomass power projects. Furthermore, recent literature suggests that large-scale adoption of negative emissions technologies such as biomass energy with carbon capture and sequestration could play an important role for reaching long-term climate stabilization targets of 2 °C proposed in the Paris Agreement (Favero and Mendelsohn, 2014, 2017). Future research is therefore needed to assess the specific sources and management of biomass feedstocks and to examine the possible effects of climate mitigation policies on biomass power plant economics and environmental performance.
